anomaly_def.Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings (memory, checkpoint, log, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to workload and hardware, creating artificial pressure or idle gaps even when raw resources are available.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying disks, array, or cloud volume have reached or exceeded their physical IOPS/MB-per-s/latency budget, so read and write requests queue and stall.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Allocated space for data, log, temp, or backup areas is nearly or completely exhausted, provoking allocation failures, auto-extend stalls, and log/archive rollover blockage.

When these three root causes co-exist, the database is simultaneously governed by counter-productive engine settings, starved for I/O bandwidth, and pressed against hard space limits. Operators observe a confusing mix of symptoms: erratic checkpoint or log-flush storms that generate surges of writes against storage already at throughput saturation; rapidly rising I/O queues and latency coupled with non-linear slowdowns in query and batch completion; frequent "out of space" or "cannot extend" errors interleaved with long write-wait times; CPU may oscillate between spin-waiting on I/O and under-utilisation due to blocked sessions; background maintenance (vacuum, defrag, compression) falls irrecoverably behind, further inflating space usage while failing to reclaim it; monitoring may show paradoxical metrics such as high log-write waits while disks appear busy and free-space alarms firing in quick succession.

Causally, poor configuration choices—such as undersized log files, aggressive checkpoint intervals, disabled async I/O, or oversized per-session work areas—inflate I/O demand and write amplification. The swollen I/O workload pushes the storage layer to its throughput ceiling, inflating latency and prolonging unit I/O operations. Prolonged I/O times slow log archiving and space reclamation, causing log segments, temp areas, and data files to accumulate and consume remaining capacity. As free space dwindles, the storage subsystem may introduce additional throttling or garbage-collection overhead, further reducing effective throughput. The cyclic feedback between mis-tuned parameters (which create bursty or excessive I/O), physical bandwidth exhaustion, and mounting space pressure quickly escalates into pervasive stalls, allocation failures, and potential service outage.

entry.official_definition: Specifies how long transmitted data may remain unacknowledged before the TCP connection is forcibly closed.
entry.trigger_condition: TCP data sent by PostgreSQL remains unacknowledged longer than tcp_user_timeout on systems supporting TCP_USER_TIMEOUT.
entry.workload_impact: The TCP connection is forcibly closed.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
